title: DOT1L activity limits transcription elongation velocity and favors RNAPII pausing to facilitate mutagenesis by AID

paper_content.abstract: Activation-induced deaminase (AID) mutates immunoglobulin genes to initiate antibody diversification by class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation but can also target non-immunoglobulin loci with oncogenic consequences. The mechanisms determining gene susceptibility to AID remain unclear. Here, we show that the H3K79 histone methyltransferase DOT1L is proximal to nuclear AID and promotes both class switch recombination and off-target AID activity, including Igh-cMyc translocations in mouse B cells. AID-mutated genes display high DOT1L activity. In the absence of DOT1L, nascent transcription largely increases despite reduced RNA Polymerase II (RNAPII) occupancy. Integrative genomic analyses reveal that DOT1L locally restricts transcription elongation velocity proportionally to H3K79me2/3 levels and extends RNAPII pausing. These transcriptional conditions enhance AID occupancy and thereby its activity. Our findings provide a harmonizing explanation for the bidirectional gene expression changes observed in DOT1L-deficient cells, and link attenuated transcriptional elongation velocity and prolonged RNAPII pausing to productive AID engagement at target loci.
paper_content.introduction:
Upon activation, B cells modify the immunoglobulin (Ig) genes to enable the production of high-affinity antibodies with distinct effector functions. The variable exons (IgV) encoding the antigen-binding domain accumulate point mutations through the process of somatic hypermutation (SHM), thereby modulating antibody affinity1. The antibody heavy chain IgH locus additionally undergoes class switch recombination (CSR) to replace the constant region that defines the isotype, thus diversifying its effector function2.

SHM and CSR are initiated by Activation-Induced Deaminase (AID), which deaminates cytosine to uracil in single-stranded DNA exposed during transcription1. SHM results from uracil processing at the IgV1. Transcription from the main IgH promoter upstream of IgV enables SHM and produces transcripts encoding IgM by default. The IgH locus contains a tandem array of independent germline transcription units (GLTUs), each comprising a cytokine-inducible promoter, a repetitive intronic switch (S)-region, and the constant region exons of each isotype2. GLTUs produce sterile transcripts that enable AID activity. Uracil processing leads to DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) simultaneously at two S-regions, triggering CSR1. While Sµ, the first S-region downstream from the IgV is constitutively transcribed, transcription of the other S-regions is controlled by cytokine signaling, enabling the B cell microenvironment to influence isotype switching3. GLTU transcription interplays with cohesin-mediated chromatin loop extrusion to bring S-regions into proximity, facilitating recombination4. We hypothesized that proteins enabling AID can also introduce mutations and DSBs in a few hundred genes in normal B cells5–11. AID-induced DSBs can lead to oncogenic chromosomal translocations involving the Ig, such as IgH-cMyc fusions12. Notably, AID occupancy is not sufficient to predict mutagenesis, indicating that additional regulatory steps determine its activity6,13,14. Genes susceptible to AID activity share transcriptional features with the Ig, including super-enhancer regulation, antisense transcription, and high occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNAPII) and its co-factor SPT57–9,15,16. We have proposed that AID activity requires a licensing step linked to the transition of RNAPII into productive elongation13, although the underlying mechanism remains unresolved.

Histone modifications may facilitate AID activity. However, the histone marks correlating with AID activity, such as H3K4me3, H3K27ac, H3K36me3, and H3K79me2, are associated with active transcription9,17–19. Dissecting whether these modifications actively promote AID activity or reflect the transcriptional state of targeted genes is not trivial.

DOT1L is the only methyltransferase producing H3K79me1, me2, and me3 via a distributive mechanism, while demethylation is thought to occur largely by nucleosome dilution20–22. B cell-specific ablation of Dot1l in mice has pleiotropic effects, hampering B cell development, germinal center formation, and humoral responses, with reduced switched antibodies but also IgM23,24. Dot1l−/− mouse B cells stimulated ex vivo have reduced IgG1 switching, supporting a B cell-intrinsic role of DOT1L in CSR, albeit the effect depended on the stimulus, and the mechanism was not explored24. DOT1L ablation or inhibition in a human B cell lymphoma line reduced SHM25. Thus, while DOT1L has been implicated in CSR and SHM24,25, and AID off-target genes have H3K79me2 among other epigenetic marks typical of high transcription9,18, whether DOT1L contributes to off-target mutations, and the underlying mechanism remain unknown.

H3K79me2/3 are associated with actively transcribed genes26–28. However, DOT1L deficiency produces relatively few gene expression changes in stem cells, and results in at least as many upregulated as downregulated genes in somatic cells22,29–31, including B cells24. Although genes with higher elongation rates are associated with higher H3K79me2 levels27,28, some evidence suggests that DOT1L may limit transcription32,33. Moreover, DOT1L activity has been proposed to regulate transcription, either positively or negatively, at either initiation34, promoter-proximal pause escape32,33, and, indirectly, elongation32,33. Moreover, DOT1L might promote transcription by methylation-independent functions in defined contexts35–37. Consequently, interpreting the role of DOT1L in AID function remains challenging for lack of consensus on how DOT1L modulates transcription at the molecular level.

Here, we identify DOT1L and the super elongation complex (SEC) as nuclear AID-proximal factors. We find that the DOT1L-MLLT10 complex promotes CSR independently of SEC components. DOT1L catalytic activity is essential for this function, implicating H3K79 methylation. DOT1L also facilitates AID off-target activity with high local DOT1L activity, marking AID-targeted genes. Mechanistically, DOT1L deficiency causes transcriptional changes indicative of increased RNAPII elongation velocity over H3K79me2/3 regions and shorter pausing. These changes coincide with reduced AID occupancy and activity. Furthermore, because increased transcription elongation velocity increases or decreases transcriptional output depending on the gene context, it could explain expression changes caused by DOT1L deficiency. Our findings reveal transcription elongation effects by DOT1L and a link between RNAPII elongation dynamics and AID activity.
paper_content.results:
DOT1L and the SEC are proximal to nuclear AID and promote CSR genome-wide

AID activity would be enriched in its vicinity in the nucleus. To identify such factors, we performed proximity-dependent biotinylation (BioID) using AID fused to the biotin ligase BirA* at either terminus (AID-BirA, BirA-AID) in Flp-In 293 TREx cells38. This approach yielded 382 preys significantly enriched over BirA-GFP and BirA controls (Supplementary Data 1).

To refine this list, we first excluded preys also identified in BioID experiments using APOBEC2, a structurally similar but functionally distinct AID paralog39. Second, we exploited the inability of BirA-AID to access the nucleus to exclude preferentially cytoplasmic interactions. AID shuttles between nucleus and cytoplasm, but large N-terminal fusions block its nuclear import40. Accordingly, both AID-BirA and BirA-AID were mainly cytoplasmic under steady state, but only AID-BirA accumulated into the nucleus upon treatment with drugs that prevent AID cytoplasmic retention and nuclear export (Supplementary Fig. 1a)40. These filters yielded 124 preys preferentially labeled by AID-BirA (Supplementary Data 1), including known AID partners (e.g., Exosome-associated NEXT complex41). We prioritized transcription-associated factors for further analysis, in particular the DOT1L complex (Fig. 1a, b). We also identified histone readers MLLT6 and MLLT10, which can associate with DOT1L29,42,43, and components of the super elongation complex (SEC), which regulates promoter-proximal pause release (Fig. 1a–c)44. The SEC consists of one scaffold protein (AFF1 or AFF4), one histone reader (MLLT1 or MLLT3), and transcription elongation factors, notably P-TEFb) (Fig. 1c)44. AFF3 forms a distinct SEC-like complex, which also recruits P-TEFb44 and supports CSR to select isotypes45. DOT1L can interact with MLLT1 or MLLT3 independently of the SEC or MLLT6/10 (Fig. 1c), suggesting multiple functionally distinct DOT1L complexes29,42,46–49.

To test the function of these complexes in CSR, we knocked down each factor in the CH12F3 mouse B cell line, which switches to IgA upon stimulation with anti-CD40, IL-4, and TGFβ-1 (CIT)50. This approach showed that DOT1L, MLLT10, MLLT1, AFF1, and AFF4 were each required for optimal CSR, without affecting cell division or AID mRNA levels, except for MLLT10 knockdown, which reduced AID by ~25% (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Fig. 1b, c). Apoptosis increased upon CIT stimulation after depletion of DOT1L, MLLT1, MLLT6, MLLT10, or AFF4 (Supplementary Fig. 1d), suggesting a protective role after acute stimuli. However, CSR was quantified in viable (DAPI-) cells and apoptosis did not correlate with CSR defects. Sµ or Sα GLT levels did not significantly change after depleting DOT1L or the SEC components contributing the most to CSR (Fig. 1e). We measured unspliced GLTs, which have <75 min half-lives and would reflect large transcriptional changes (Supplementary Fig. 1e).

We conclude that DOT1L, MLLT10, MLLT1, AFF1, AFF3, and AFF4 are proximal to nuclear AID and have non-redundant contributions to CSR.

DOT1L functions independently of the SEC in CSR

Because DOT1L and the SEC can function cooperatively, and MLLT1/3 can be part of either complex49, we performed epistasis analysis to determine whether DOT1L acts with or independently of the SEC in CSR. We inactivated Dot1l in two parental WT CH12F3 populations to obtain two independent clones with identical homozygous in-frame deletions in the DOT1L methyltransferase domain (Dot1lΔ/Δ-1 and Dot1lΔ/Δ-2), as well as a Dot1l−/− clone with frameshifting deletions that truncate the protein at amino acid ~100 (Supplementary Fig. 2a). Although no antibody detected mouse DOT1L, the protein variant potentially produced by Dot1lΔ/Δ clones had no effect on CSR when overexpressed in WT CH12F3 cells, excluding dominant-negative activity

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The manuscript by Subramani et al connects transcription regulation by DOT1L to the initiation of class switch recombination (CSR) of antibody genes and “off-target” effects of Activation-induced deaminase (AID). The authors identify DOT1L as a protein “proximal” to AID in Flp-In 293 TREx cells and then use the CH12F3 mouse cell line derived from B cell lymphoma for most of the subsequent analyses. Several DOT1L mutant derivatives of CH12F3 have been generated and experiments comparing WT (lymphoma) and DOT1L mutant conditions have been performed. shRNA knockdown of DOT1L was used as an additional alternative approach. The authors report diminished CSR frequency, reduced off-target AID-dependent mutations, and elevated Pol II pause-release upon DOT1L loss. Since Pol II pausing favors AID activity the major conclusion of the paper is that DOT1L affects AID through its regulation of transcription elongation.

The strength of this work is in using several DOT1L mutant alleles and revealing the effect of the mutations on CSR and off-target AID activity leading to gene fusions. Also, the effects of DOT1L on cohesin distribution are interesting. In this regard, does the downregulation of cohesin affect CSR?

The weaknesses:
1. The focus on DOT1L singled out among the numerous AID prays is not well justified. DOT1L complexes specific for cells used in functional analyses are not investigated.
2. Lack of direct connection between DOT1L and loci subject to CSR. Since DOT1L has a global effect on transcription, the indirect role of DOT1L in CSR cannot be excluded.
3. Claiming the discovery of Pol II pause-release regulation by DOT1L, despite the pioneering C. elegans study in 2013. Notably, a study using an ESCs reprogramming system showed a functional role for DOT1L-regulated Pol II pause-release of housekeeping genes (Wille et al. 2022, BioRxiv), like the C. elegans work.
4. Results, such as in Figure 3 “Dot1l regulates GLTs expression fidelity” and Figure 5 “Global alteration in transcription output caused by Dot1l loss” touch upon complex subjects that are not well integrated into the main storyline. Figure 3 results are related to the regulation of gene expression plasticity by several factors, including DOT1L, which was comprehensively described in the Xiao et al Open Biology 2019 publication. The Figure 5 subject is complex and not limited to the role of DOT1L in Pol II pause release. There is literature connecting DOT1L to enhancer regulation through effects on chromatin compaction, as well as studies connecting DOT1L to antisense transcription regulation. This was not properly referenced in the paper.
I do not find conclusions that gene length affects the mode of transcription regulation by DOT1L (UP or DOWN) particularly convincing, this part should be removed from the model in Figure 8 (or from the manuscript altogether). Data analyses based on gene function might be more informative, especially if related to the main story of the manuscript.
The authors relate their Pol II pause-release findings to literature about known pausing factors and their inhibitors: Spt5, RN7SK, NELF, PAF1, etc. This is not justified by the results. Unless they do experiments and implicate these factors in CSR, they must instead focus on the similarity of their DOT1L findings to the C. elegans system that lacks NELF and the Wille et al. 2022, BioRxiv publication.
5. The introduction gives no background about DOT1L and the current state of our understanding of its effect(s) on transcription and chromatin organization.

Specific issues:
Figure 4A, C: How does total RNA Pol II distribution look in Dot1l +/- conditions? It is expected to change.
Figure 4B, bottom: Why ChIP-qPCR at the P region is not shown?
Figure 4C: Analyses using randomized groups of genes with the same # should be performed for control.
Figure 4F: Show expression changes corresponding to each group of genes.
Figure 6 A, C: The difference between H3K79me3 distribution in splenic B cells and CH12F3 cells is concerning and must be addressed. How do these profiles look in unstimulated cells?
Figure S2 B: Why does CIT lead to H3K79me reduction?
Triplicate replicates should be shown for all RT-qPCR and ChIP-qPCR data.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this paper, the authors investigate the mechanism of DOT1L promoting AID-induced class switch recombination (CSR) as well as “off-target” mutations. They applied BioID to identify nuclear AID-proximal proteins that potentially contribute to AID-induced mutations. From the results, they identified DOT1L and its associated proteins, as well as SEC as being specifically enriched in the AID interacting complex. To evaluate the function of DOT1L they perform knockdown and knockout experiments and find that CSR is inconsistently affected at germ line transcripts depending on locus and method of knockout. Since the local effects at IgH do not show a trend based on characteristics of accumulated chromatin marks, they then perform RNAPII ChIP-seq from which they conclude a correlation between promoter pause release and H3K79me3 enrichment. Finally they perform experiments on cohesion accumulation that suggest a link It has been reported that DOT1L is essential for B cell differentiation, but the authors provide insights into the potential mechanisms that may be relevant.

Major points:
1. The first major claim of the manuscript is that DOT1L has a role in CSR ( Fig 1-3 )- which has been reported before (EMBO Rep. from the Leeuwen lab). In that prior paper it was shown that DOT1L promotes somatic hypermutation and lowered RNA Pol II occupancy at immunoglobulin variable region.
1.1 The results in this manuscript are inconsistent with the prior published results (Fig 1E showed a different result at the same locations (Su)) and at different regions where shDOT1L can both increase or decrease RNAPII occupancy (Fig 1E).
1.2 The effects of the DOT1L binding partner MLLT10 on class switching (Fig 1K) are undermined by the lack of substantial knockdown at 48 hours (Fig S1C). Further, In Fig 1K, shAID further reduced CSR I the background of DOT1L deficiency, indicating DOT1L is not necessary for AID function.
1.3 The CH12F3 delta/delta lines and the CH12F3 delta/- lines of DOT1L deletion are different from each other – The delta/delta lines retain frame (Fig S2A)- which means there is a DOT1l truncation mutant protein that could act as a dominant negative. DOT1L KO lines need a DOT1L western blot to confirm the protein is deleted.
This is an important consideration because the results in Fig 2A are misinterpreted by pooling the samples from both kinds of deletions on CSR ( triangles and squares in the bar graphs).
1.4 The effects of DOT1L deletion on GLTs are inconsistent and modest at different loci, between different kinds of DOT1L deletion and in resting and activated conditions ( for example In Fig 3C, expression of lghg2c is increased in stimulated condition but decreased in resting state upon DOT1L KO).
Further in Fig2A, 2H and 3A, GLT changes do not correlate with reduced CSR or transcription elongation defects. Then DOT1L inhibition upregulates unscheduled GLTs cannot be the mechanism of DOT1L regulates CSR.
While the authors argue for complex regulation by DOT1L for CSR, the data could also support a minor role for DOT1L that is far downstream of other players. For example in the mass spectrometry in addition to DOT1L, the H3K4 methyltransferase is also specifically enriched. This result would suggest that that the proteins interacting with AID are proximal to the transcription start site and not specific to AID. AID-ChIP at GLT loci in DOT1L deletion lines could be a method to support DOT1L deletion affects CSR through interaction with AID.
1.5 Statistical tests are inconsistently applied across Figs 1-3 ( for example between the two kinds of DOT1L deleted lines in Fig 1H), in several cases there are only 2 replicates- it is not indicated whether the replicates are technical or biological , and standard error of mean is used instead of std deviation from mean. There are missing error bars and significance testing ( Fig S3C is missing error bars in some timepoints and in certain axis. S3D needs significance test).
2. The second major claim of the manuscript is that DOT1L acts by limiting pause release and not transcription elongation, and that leads to transcriptional upregulation.
2.1 First it is argued that the total RNAPII CUT&RUN signal is lower in DOT1L KO cells because of the epitope being masked by high S2P-RNAPII, but it is also argued there are no global changes in cellular levels of RNAPII or S2P-PolII which is impossible to interpret because Fig. S4B does not have a loading control. Total Pol II CHIP PCR for other GLT locations in 4B in WT/KO lines would also help observations on pause-release differences related to gene expression changes from Fig 3 and H3K79me levels.
2.2 At the locus specific level Fig 4B – the total RNAPII enrichment differences are modest, the S2P-RNAPII enrichment at the promoter is not presented- this leads to the question of whether there is a nonspecific increase of S2P-RNAPII everywhere . The intergenic region ( bottom panel of Fig 4B) does not serve as a control for this question because the enrichment at that location is a magnitude lower than that at the Sgamma3 location.
2.3 Most disconcertingly it is argued that the RNAP C-terminal antibody is unreliable- yet it is the one used for calculating the pausing index (Fig 4E and 4F).
2.4 The ChIP-seq of H3K79me3 could also include H3K79me2 location as in Fig4A, 4C, 6C, 6B, the signal of H3K79me2 and H3K79me3 show almost the same pattern. Further, between Fig 6B and S5A, H3K79me2 ChIP displays very different patterns between mouse splenic B cells and CH12F3 cell line.
In the clustering of H3K79me3 levels (Fig 4C) most genes with estimated traveling ratios are in the first 2 quintiles. It is unclear why H3K79me3 quantification at TSS site is used for correlation to the pausing index since this location is not representative of general H3K79me3 distributions in the gene body. The conclusion that pause-release is related to H3K79me3 levels, would be more convincing if other features such as H3K79me1/2 and gene expression level are not corelated with the pausing index.
2.5 In Fig 5G & S4H H3K4me3 has 2 populations- and every pairwise comparison is statistically significant – if that is the case then the distribution of H3K4me3 cannot causal for transcriptional changes.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript of Subramani and co-workers entitled "DOT1L limits RNAPII promoter-proximal pause release thus enabling Activation Induced Deaminase activity genome-wide" deals with the molecular underpinnings of class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation of antibody genes, which involves the action of Activation induced deaminase (AID). But the data extend towards genome-wide analysis with the intention to generalize some of the findings. The authors discover that AID interacts with DOT1L and they embarked to characterize how AID and DOT1L mediate CSR and SHM, and whether DOT1L is involved in AID off-target deamination.
In all this is very impressive and experimental rich work that proposes novel mechanisms of action for the histone methyltransferase DOT1L. My main concern about the data presentation in its present form is that it should worked out much clearer - especially for the broader scientific community - how the different proposed mechanisms are linked to either genome-wide and/or IgH-specific transcriptional control. In its present form the proposed mechanisms are not always presented in a connected form but rather independent from each other.
Major points:
1) The authors show that it is DOT1L and not, indirectly, the super elongation complex that accounts for CSR, although the SEC was also part of the interactome.
As later in the manuscript the authors show increased S2P-RNAPolII in the gene bodies upon DOT1L deletion, a stronger activity of the SEC might be likely. It would be good, if this aspect could be validated as well. Along the same line, showing a concomitant decrease in S5P-RNAPolII as the pausing form would also be direct proof, that the switch from pausing to elongating is affected by the action of DOT1L (or its interaction partners).
In the same setting some experiments and their interpretation might need clarification:
- is the SEC increased (expression levels? occupancy (esp. in regard to the S2P RNAPII accumulation shown in Fig. 4C)? interaction with AID?) upon DOT1L deletion? And why would this be? Is there an increase in Dot1L or the relevant SEC components as well after CIT? Is there increased interaction between DOT1L and AID in this condition?
- Dot1L is as Mllt1 not depleted but rather increased in Fig. 1E for Su. Please comment.
- In regard to the AID interactions with SEC or DOT1L: Do the components sit there and wait for AID to come in? Or is AID recruiting? Or is AID being recruited? What is the dynamics in the system?
2) In regard to placing the action of DOT1L up- or downstream of break formation: How do the authors explain that increased NHEJ occurs upon deletion of the catalytic domain of DOT1L in the delta/delta-1 clones, but unchanged NHEJ upon use to of the inhibitor?
This observation is not leading to the (sole) conclusion given, that "Dot1l acts at or upstream of the break formation step in CSR". It rather suggests that the scaffolding function of DOT1L would be involved - and it would be interesting to learn what this function would be.
3) The authors use H3K79me2 or me3 as readout for DOT1L activity, however it is not entirely clear that the mark itself is implicated in the process. Rather, the scaffolding function of DOT1L or activity towards other protein targets might also explain some of the observations. Thus, it is necessary to show that DOT1L is indeed present at the IgH loci itself (in the context of Fig. 2), not only the marks, which might be secondary or not necessary for the function. Also, it needs to be shown that the catalytic deletion protein localizes similarly or not - or to use point mutations for inactivation to dissect clearly whether it is the mark or the scaffold.
The same is true for the statement in regard to Fig. 3B and S3F, S5A - is Dot1l present at these loci in a defined, sequence specific manner (not at Sy1, Se but on Syb, Sy3, Sy2c and Sa) - or is this finding of different methylation levels a coincidence of a locus-wide general activity and deposition of the mark?
4) The authors observed that the enzymatic activity would be important for CSR; and it seems that also the pausing of RNAPolII correlates to this observation. Thus, is it sufficient to inhibit DOt1L to observe similar effects as shown in Fig. 4? However, the statement "we conclude that the H3K79 methylation limits promoter-proximal pause escape genome-wide including the IgH GLTUs" seems correlative. For being substantiated, it would need further experimentation to support this claim: e.g. gradual loss of H3k79me3 towards me2, me1 which should then release RNA Poll pausing. Or locus-specific non-methylation using dCas9 constructs. And if this is a claim to be generalized in terms of DOT1L function - i.e. independent on the Ig-locus CSR - this correlation should be observable in other cell systems as well. Which has to be demonstrated.
In addition the Chip profiles focusing at the IgH GLTUs might be good to provide in 4C to support the claim "including the IgH GLTUs".
5) The authors conclude from their study that "DOT1L activity enables genome-wide AID off-target activity" - however, for me it is not entirely clear which mechanism is responsible despite that multiple were proposed, including
*paused Pol II release upon loss of Dot1l
*H3K4me1/me3 levels
*CTCF/cohesin loop extrusion
As the off-target activity of AID was suggested to be the main focus of the study, I would have expected to have a clearer picture on the mechanism in this regard.
6) In the discussion the authors mention other inhibitors/deletions that alter RNAPII pausing. If indeed the pausing is the mechanism behind CSR, it would be interesting to know if these inactivations/deletions (of RN7SK, Spt5) also affect the CSR events observed here? Showing such correlation would be a strong claim towards the pausing as major mechanism.
On the other hand, the authors claim that "H3K79 methylation might maintain the balance of these kinase and phosphatase activities in situ". How should this happen - and would this not need to be studied in order to provide the necessary mechanistic insights?
Minor points:
1) Figures of quantifications vary in showing single data points or not - please add single data points in coherent way to all figures. Please also indicate the individual n numbers used for each experiment within the legends.
It seems that some experiments are displayed with a n=2 (i.e. S2E, F,H). Even if this data in included "only" in the supplemental data - is it sufficient to interpret the experiment without proper statistical testing?
Along this line comes Fig. 2A, 3D, which is problematic, as first of all two experiments with different cell lines are combined in one bar, and variable numbers of experiments are shown (even within the combination of different cell lines). It seems that for CD4 only two data points are shown (this is why the legend should contain all n numbers, as this can also be a graphical problem). Please separate the experiments and provide valid statistical evaluation.
2) Fig. S2B: what is the reason for showing me2 for two loci and me3 for three? A coherent representation would be much more convincing. Along the line is the representation of the GLT exons: What is Sy1 and why is this not shown for me3? The Sy1 fragment is not mentioned in the text or legend, and I think the schemes are also not depicting the fragment explicitly (also relevant for Fig.3A, where other Sy's show up).
3) Fig. 1G: show H3K79me3 as well
4) In the context of Fig. 4: That Pinometostat is not influencing AID expression is not necessarily corroborated by the blots presented - a slight increase in protein levels might be present. The authors might want to quantify this effect (accompanied by a power analysis to determine the numbers of samples they would need to analyze - as the effect seems rather small) to support this claim, which is central to discriminate between the methylation activity towards H3 or acting as scaffold.
5) The authors conclude in line 236/237 that "determines a transcriptional environment that enables AID activity,...". The authors might to make this statement more precise and describe how this environment would look like and how it impacts on AID activity. The link between transcription (other than presence of RNAPII) and AID activity is not easy to appreciate - even if it might be within the data.
6) The authors cite that "Loss of H3K27me3 has been proposed to explain gene upregulation in Dot1l-deficient cells, but this mark was absent from the Igh...". Another paper showing EZH2/DOT1L crosstalk was recently published (Appiah et al. 2023, EmboRep), making this point important to substantiate in this system. If H3K27me3 is not present at the IgH locus, is H3K27ac maybe enriched? How is the epigenetic landscape changing, maybe also in regard to ATAC seq, in Dot1l deficient cells?
7) Fig. 4B: The P side in SerP2 chip could serve as a negative control. Statistics is missing in the figure as well as representation of individual data points.
8) Line 254: In the context of Fig. 4 the authors conclude "Collectively, these results suggested increased promoter-proximal pause release in the Dot1l-deficient cells for those GLTUs that were open and preloaded with RNAPII." The openness of the locus was not experimentally addressed.
9) Line 257: "Since we identified DOT1L proximal to AID by BioID, we expected that any role of DOT1L found at the IgH might be conserved genome-wide"
I do not understand this rationale. Please make it clearer. For me it would still be possible that the AID/switching is locus specific (admittantly for me this is more plausible then a genome wide mechanism).
10) For the definition of the quantiles according to H3K79me3: what is the rationale to use H3K79me3 and not H3K79me2?
Please make clear to the reader.
11) The authors observe an increase of RNAPII-S2P in the gene bodies - the scaling in Fig. 4C is probably distance from TSS and goes up to 120kb - an accumulation in the gene body is hardly visible in this present form, as it is not indicated in the figure - isn't a representation that spans TSS to TES better suited to show the distributions? At least as an additional representation, as I understand that the drop at 40kb becomes relevant later.
12) The experiments concerning distribution of RNAPII and its phosphorylated form by means of the two antibodies used, are a little confusing and difficult to perceive - this might need better explanation. Within Fig. S4C the enrichment is given as % of input and this is (much) lower for N20 then for 8WG16. Please explain this discrepancy.
Probably the authors would like to point towards the delta between the two conditions - however this can be variable between experiments as for N20 a N=2 is displayed, and for 8WG16 the N number is not given.
Thus - in the present representation of the results, it might be a real effect that is observed here - and this might be in favor of a locus specific observation opposing the claim of a general genome-wide phenomenon?
13) Fig. 4C indicates an increased/accumulated signal of S2P RNA PII in the 3' end of the genes. How is this explained?
What is trapping S2P RNAPII at this location - is there a problem in transcriptional termination?
14) Line 315: why does the conclusion not contain the K4me1/me3 ratio that suggests a similar high correlation than the paused PolII?
The statement on the altered ratio of the K4 methylation somehow comes out of the blue - there is no ChIP seq profiles or ChIP qPCRs that address this point of H3K4me1/me3. But this seems highly relevant as mechanism and probably contributing to the RNAPII S2P escape from pausing.
15) Please clarify the molecular definition of the stripe in regard to the marks/factors shown in Fig. 6A; and indicate selection of super enhancers and or criteria in the selection.
Spelling/phrasing and other mistakes:
line 69: "However, determining the underlying mechanisms or these histone marks are necessary for AID activity"
line 106: Please add a citation - and maybe make stronger the hypothesis that the complexes have been proposed as being mutually exclusive ("We also identified several histone readers that can form a complex with DOT1L but are also components of the super elongation complex (SEC)")
line 132: "and are participate in CSR".
line 198: Papers 47, 48 are not describing demethylation - the citation seems not appropriate. In addition - the cited papers explicitly excluded the study of human Dot1l which seems not to follow the behavior of lower eucaryotes.
Fig. S4F: DGE or DEG?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Activation Induced Deaminase (AID) is an essential factor that drives somatic hypermutation and class switch recombination in B Cells leading to antibody diversification. It is well accepted that AID mutates single strand DNA (ssDNA) sequences to generate point mutations during SHM (V gene sequence mutations) and DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) to cause CSR. In the process of catalyzing CSR and SHM, AID also incorporates SHM all across the B Cell genome (although at a much lower frequency), these mutations are related with occurrence of germinal center derived B cell lymphomas. A puzzling and important question is how does AID identify various DNA target sequences, at V genes and its target DNA sequence across the B cell genome. Many past studies have related AID activity with transcription states both at sense and antisense direction, secondary DNA structures like R-loops and G4s (that form during transcription), epigenetics and genome architecture formation, etc. In this study, the Subramani et al. proposes that the H3K79me1/2/3 inducing enzymes DOT1L induces AID recruitment to the B cell genome. The authors also propose that DOT1L functions with a similar mechanism to cause CSR, DOT1L deficient CH12F3 lines are also deficient in CSR. The authors show that DOT1L induces RNA polII promoter proximal pausing to accumulate RNA polII at AID target DNA sequences to induce AID recruitment (AID binds to RNA polII robustly and thus this is the likely mechanism). In this regard, the authors show that in absence of DOT1L promoter proximal paused RNA polII levels decrease but S2 phosphorylated elongating RNA polII increases in the gene body. Thus, this study also makes the argument that S2 phosphorylated RNA polII is unlikely to recruit AID. Although some previous studies (cited in the manuscript) have investigated and shown DOT1L’s role in AID recruitment and CSR, neither of these two studies suggested mechanisms similar to that proposed in this manuscript. Please find below some suggestions that the authors could consider as they revise the manuscript for publication. Overall, I feel this manuscript advances the field of AID biology and also provide insights into transcription and promoter-proximal pausing mechanism.
1. In figure 1, authors present a nice assay with AID-BirA approach for AID interacting proteins. Some highlights of AID interaction with the NEXT complex and MRN complex was not discussed in the text. NEXT subunits functionally interact with AID has been shown before and with regards to AID activity regulation (Lim et al, 2017). Similarly, the interaction with MRN is also relevant for discussion.
2. The inability of AID to stimulate CSR is an important marker for functional aspect of its cofactors, in cells that are deleted/hypomorphic of cofactor activity. In Fig. 1A versus 1K, the authors show different efficiencies of CSR in DOT1L deleted cells (50% versus less that 30%). Some clarity will help since this assay does decide how important DOT1L is for AID activity (at least during CSR).
3. This maybe a confusion on my part, but it is not clear to me why in Fig. 4A the H3K79me2/3 ChIP-seq data for DOTL1-/- cells were not shown. The parallel demonstration of the tracks will make it clear that the mutant cells are deprived of DOT1L activity and still undergo robust transcription (RNA polII levels) and elongation (S2PRNA polII levels).
4. The most striking observation in this study is the effect of DOT1L inhibition on AID off-targeting and IgH-myc translocations (Fig. 7 and S6). The authors find with chemical inhibition of DOT1L (chemical inhibition is well characterized with all proper controls), the authors report decreased translocations (fig. 7E). Myc-translocations occur at promoters and also in gene body and the PVT1 locus downstream in humans. What translocations are the ones the authors are mapping, are these Myc promoter translocations, some details with sequencing data of the translocation site would be helpful. Fig. 7E could be done from two different mice (instead of B cells from one mouse). Pinemetostat treatment may decrease IgH-Myc translocations at promoters, but does the translocations move to a new site (some bands are seen in the gel).
5. The authors discuss that H3K79me3 modifications occur 5 Kb away from the TSS (Fig. 7A), but SHM and promoter proximal pausing occurs in the first 1 kb and 100 bps, respectively. This could be clarified.
6. The model in Fig. 8 and the associated discussion could be improved. Based on my understanding of this study, DOT1L restricts PolII residence time in a promoter proximal paused state, thereby recruiting AID and increasing SHM. Previous studies have supported the fact that bidirectionally transcribed regulatory DNA sequences (like in promoters and enhancers) accumulate AID activity and those studies support the conclusions of this manuscript (Pefanis et al, 2014; Meng et al, 2014; Qian et al, 2014). These DNA regulatory sequences have accumulated promoter proximal pausing and are most likely be regulated with DOT1L activity. Authors should consider them in the discussion. The authors could also described SHM (following DOT1L inhibition) at some of the off-target genes whose transcription was measured and shown to increase (Fig. S6). This study does highlight that increased transcript levels at AID target sites is not always proportional to mutagenic activity of the protein. These observations are consistent with previously published studies where it has been shown that increase in switch region transcripts or at AID off target genes does not always lead to increase AID mediated DNA mutagenesis. These published studies should be discussed and considered in the revision.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
This manuscript examines the role of the H3K79 methyltransferase Dot1L in transcription, class switch recombination (CSR), and AID mistargeting in the genome. The authors identify Dot1L and other factors including components of the super elongation complex as AID proximity factors in 293 cells. As the authors summarize, it was previously known that Dot1L contributes to efficient CSR and somatic hypermutation (SHM), but the mechanism of action was unknown. The authors also nicely summarize previous findings linking Dot1L to defects in transcription and point out the limitations in those findings. This study substantially extends previous work by showing that Dot1L regulates transcription by restraining Pol2 promoter proximal pause release (PPPR). The substantial data presented here and the similarities with findings from other factors that negatively regulate PPPR provide a strong argument that the catalytic activity of Dot1L (and likely H3K79me2/me3) help restrict PPPR. This and the other findings related to the effects of Dot1L on transcription are the main strength of the manuscript.
The authors also make the claim (last sentence of abstract) that their findings have established that regulated pause release is “a critical step for AID activity”. We do not agree. While the findings strengthen the link between Dot1L (and its catalytic activity) and CSR and AID targeting, they do not establish mechanism. Specifically, the findings establish a correlation between Dot1L-regulated Pol2 PPPR and CSR/AID targeting, not a causal link. One alternative explanation among others is that methylated H3K79 is the key contribution of Dot1L, not the regulation of PPPR. We feel that the mechanistic advance offered by this study regarding the role of Dot1L in CSR/AID targeting is significant but not definitive. This is the primary limitation of the study. We emphasize that we find their model attractive and plausible; it simply hasn’t been established. Is this required for publication in Nature Communications? That’s a judgement call, though overall we would support publication without a requirement for substantial additional experiments. At minimum, the manuscript needs to be rewritten to remove overly strong mechanistic claims and to address alternative hypotheses.
If the authors decide to try to strengthen the link between dysregulated PPPR and AID targeting, they might attempt to identify a factor(s) that reduces CSR/AID targeting and alters PPPR similarly to Dot1L but does not reduce levels of methylated H3K79—this would substantially strengthen the correlation and argue against a primary role for methylated H3K79. Their study identifies several candidates for study, e.g., SEC components.
In other regards, the study is rigorous, thorough, and well written (which we appreciated; a pleasure to read). The experiments are well designed and controlled, caveats are noted and addressed, and conclusions are carefully stated for the most part. The Discussion is well crafted to put the findings in the context of other work.
We were unable to identify many other weaknesses with this study. Minor points for consideration are:
1. Line 76: it was unclear what the phrase “strongly correlating with normal H3K79 methylation levels” refers to. Please rewrite.
2. Line 155: where are the data to support this statement?
3. Line 191: “Since switching to IgA in CH12F3 cells required Dot1l activity”; this claim is overly strong, since it implies that CSR is completely eliminated in the absence of Dot1l activity. A similar inappropriate use of the word “required” occurs on line 26 (Abstract).
4. Something wrong in the plot of H3K27Ac in S5A: big blocks of purple below the axis.
5. Line 333 and this paragraph: it is hard to appreciate the changes in the vicinity of Vh and Emu given the scale of Fig. 6B; a blow-up of this region in a supplementary figure would be helpful.
6. Grammatical errors, missing words, or typos were found on the following lines (thank you for numbering the lines): 69, 132, 190, 354, 399-400.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Point by point response
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript by Subramani et al connects transcription regulation by DOT1L to the initiation of class
switch recombination (CSR) of antibody genes and “off-target” effects of Activation-induced deaminase
(AID). The authors identify DOT1L as a protein “proximal” to AID in Flp-In 293 TREx cells and then use the
CH12F3 mouse cell line derived from B cell lymphoma for most of the subsequent analyses. Several DOT1L
mutant derivatives of CH12F3 have been generated and experiments comparing WT (lymphoma) and
DOT1L mutant conditions have been performed. shRNA knockdown of DOT1L was used as an additional
alternative approach. The authors report diminished CSR frequency, reduced off-target AID-dependent
mutations, and elevated Pol II pause-release upon DOT1L loss. Since Pol II pausing favors AID activity the
major conclusion of the paper is that DOT1L affects AID through its regulation of transcription elongation.
The strength of this work is in using several DOT1L mutant alleles and revealing the effect of the mutations
on CSR and off-target AID activity leading to gene fusions. Also, the effects of DOT1L on cohesin distribution
are interesting.
In this regard, does the downregulation of cohesin affect CSR?
The role of chromatin loop extrusion by cohesin in facilitating CSR is well established (Thomas-
Claudepierre et al, 2013; Zhang et al, 2019). Transcriptional activation of Igh germline transcript units
(GLTUs) in response to cytokine signaling leads to increased cohesin occupancy across the Igh locus
(Zhang et al, 2019; Costea et al, 2023).
We note that new data in the revised manuscript (TT-seq and additional ChIP-seq) indicate that DOT1L
regulates transcriptional elongation velocity. Given the known influence of transcriptional activity on
cohesin dynamics, the moderate change in cohesin distribution in DOT1L-deficient cells is most likely an
indirect consequence of transcriptional changes at the H3K79me2/3-rich GLTUs. In turn, chromatin loop
extrusion alterations can explain the modest activation of internal H3K79me2/3-poor unscheduled GLTUs,
as originally proposed. We make this point succinctly in Fig. 4, S5.
The weaknesses:
1. The focus on DOT1L singled out among the numerous AID prays is not well justified.
We appreciate the reviewer’s concern regarding the focus on DOT1L and have modified the text to better
explain the knowledge gaps on DOT1L and AID targeting that we are addressing.
When we initially identified DOT1L as an AID-proximal protein, it had not yet been functionally implicated
in antibody diversification. We chose to focus on DOT1L in part because prior studies had reported an
enrichment of H3K79me2 at AID target loci (Wang et al, 2014; Álvarez-Prado et al, 2018). At the time,
this modification was interpreted as a mere marker of transcriptional elongation, and the potential
mechanistic relevance of DOT1L in AID activity had not been explored.
While our work was ongoing, other studies were published demonstrating a requirement for DOT1L in
CSR and SHM. However, these reports neither tested whether DOT1L enabled AID off-target activity, nor
provided a mechanistic explanation for how DOT1L supports AID activity at the Ig loci. We sought to
answer these important outstanding questions.
In the revised manuscript, we modified the Introduction to eliminate the “discovery” aspect and better
justify the rationale to study DOT1L based on the gaps in knowledge.
components which can interact with DOT1L. Once the epistasis analysis included in the manuscript
showed that SEC and DOT1L contribute independently to CSR, the focus remains on DOT1L. We are
investigating the role and mechanism of the SEC, which is a story on its own.
DOT1L complexes specific for cells used in functional analyses are not investigated.
While we did not perform biochemical isolation and identification of DOT1L complexes in CH12F3 cells,
our functional data does provide insight into their composition and relevance.
Specifically, our epistasis analysis indicates that DOT1L cooperates with MLLT10, but not with MLLT1 or
AFF1, in promoting CSR in CH12 cells. This is further supported by our structure-function analyses, which
are consistent with the same interpretation. These data provide indirect evidence regarding the functional
complexes operating in this B cell line, i.e. DOT1L/MLLT10 on one side and the SEC acting independently
of DOT1L. Thus, our data provide meaningful mechanistic insights about the DOT1L complex in CH12 cells
2. Lack of direct connection between DOT1L and loci subject to CSR. Since DOT1L has a global effect on
transcription, the indirect role of DOT1L in CSR cannot be excluded.
We acknowledge this important point. The possibility of indirect effects is an inherent caveat when
analyzing transcription-associated chromatin modifiers and applies to prior studies linking DOT1L to CSR
and SHM, which did not establish a direct mechanistic connection. The revised manuscript provides
several lines of new evidence that strongly support a direct link between DOT1L activity and local AID
activity at the Igh locus for CSR, and at off-target genes.
i. Correlation between DOT1L activity and AID activity: We show that AID target genes are distinctly
enriched in H3K79me3 relative to equally transcribed non-target genes in both primary B cells and CH12
cells (Fig. 3A–D). We also provide data showing that the level of AID activity at individual genomic loci in
CH12 cells is approximately proportional to their H3K79me3 content (new Fig. 3D). As CDADC1 is a
distributive enzyme, higher order H3K79 methylation indicates locally higher DOT1L activity. These data
support a locus-specific requirement for DOT1L activity that is more consistent with a direct than a merely
global transcriptional effect.
ii. Functional occupancy of DOT1L at the Igh locus: We performed ChIP-qPCR experiments in CH12 cells
reconstituted with either WT or catalytically inactive DOT1L. Both forms of DOT1L are recruited to the Igh
locus (new Fig. 2B), yet only WT DOT1L can complement the CSR defect (Fig. 2A), again consistent with
local DOT1L catalytic activity supporting CSR, and ruling out potential scaffold functions.
iii. The CSR machinery remains intact in DOT1L-deficient cells: We systematically examined the
expression of genes encoding the CSR machinery in both primary B cells and CH12 cells lacking DOT1L and
found few differences in primary and no differences in CH12 cells (new Fig. S4E). AID protein levels were
unaffected (Figs. 1F, 2D, 2G). Furthermore, we demonstrate that DOT1L-deficient CH12 cells can still
undergo CSR when double-strand breaks are introduced by CRISPR targeting (Figs. S2G, S2I), indicating
that downstream components of the CSR pathway are functional. These results argue against a model in
which DOT1L indirectly affects CSR via disruption of the general CSR machinery.
iv. Transcription dynamics explain loss of AID targeting: New data in the revised manuscript show that
loss of DOT1L causes increased transcription elongation rate in a manner that is directly correlated with
H3K79me2/3 levels (new Fig. 5). Moreover, AID target genes have not only high H3K79me2/3 (Fig. 3D),
2
but the H3K79me2/3 peak overlapping the region where SHM accumulates (Fig. 3E), which is where
velocity changes the most in Dot1l-deficien cells (Fig. 5E-F).
Together, these data provide multiple converging lines of evidence that DOT1L directly facilitates AID
activity through a locus-specific, enzymatic effect on chromatin that modulates transcription dynamics.
Faster elongation provides a mechanistic explanation for the reduced AID occupancy we find at the Ig and
off targets upon DOT1L loss. These points are summarized in the revised Discussion.
3. Claiming the discovery of Pol II pause-release regulation by DOT1L, despite the pioneering C. elegans
study in 2013. Notably, a study using an ESCs reprogramming system showed a functional role for DOT1L-
regulated Pol II pause-release of housekeeping genes (Wille et al. 2022, BioRxiv), like the C. elegans work.
We apologize if we appeared to claim more than was due about pause release. This was not our intention.
We have modified the manuscript to ensure fair recognition of previous work.
However, additional data and analyses have clarified the effect of DOT1L on transcription and made us
reconsider our initial model. Our new data indicates that the effect on pausing is secondary to an increase
in transcription elongation rate over the H3K792/3-enriched intragenic regions. Our data can help
reconciling papers that detected an effect of DOT1L loss on pause release (Cecere et al, 2013; Wille et al,
2023), and others that did not (Wu et al, 2021; Cao et al, 2020), via traveling ratio calculations.
We realized that the genome wide S2P-RNAPII increase was an artifact of the spike-in normalization we
originally used for ChIP-seq data. After performing more extensive confirmatory ChIP-qPCR at the Igh and
other H3K79me2/3-high loci, we failed to see any increase (Fig S6B, S7D) (except at the unscheduled
GLTUs, which is a particular case). Moreover, western blotting did not show any quantitative changes in
RNAPII, S2P-RNAPII, and S5-RNAPII between WT and DOT1L-deficient cells (new Fig. S6B). Thus, we ruled
out a global change in S2P-RNAPII. Based on this, we reanalyzed ChIP-seq data using library size
normalization.
In addition, we have now replaced the RNAPII CUT&RUN data with RNAPII ChIP-seq, for a more accurate
calculation of pausing index, and performed TT-seq to measure nascent transcription, which offers a
temporal component to analyze kinetics. Combined with RNAPII ChIP-seq, TT-seq enabled the calculation
of elongation rate and the pause duration at the promoter-proximal region (Gressel et al, 2017; Velychko
et al, 2024).
WT and Dot1l-deficient cells showed no change in pausing index between when calculating traveling ratio
from RNAPII ChIP-seq data (Fig. S6D), as observed by others in leukemic cells (Wu et al, 2021; Cao et al,
2020). However, calculating pause duration from TT-seq and RNAPII data, shows reduced pausing time in
Dot1l-deficient cells (Fig. 5D), which is consistent with the findings mentioned by the reviewer (Cecere et
al, 2013; Wille et al, 2023). Transcription elongation velocity offers an explanation to harmonize the
apparently different effect on pausing. We find that elongation velocity is increased in Dot1l-deficient cell.
This increase is proportional to and spatially overlaps with, H3K79me3 abundance (Fig. 5E), thus most
likely reflecting a direct effect of DOT1L. In contrast, since the pausing site is relatively poor in
H3K79me2/3, we propose that shorter pause duration in DOT1L deficient cells is a consequence of faster
elongation, leading to more frequent release. This indirect effect may sometimes produce a detectable
reduction in traveling ratio, as in (Cecere et al, 2013; Wille et al, 2023), or not, as in (Wu et al, 2021; Cao
et al, 2020) and our Dot1l-deficient CH12F3 cells.
We make these points in the revised Discussion to contextualize our findings, which are complementary
to those of Cecere et al and Wille et al.
3
4. Results, such as in Figure 3 “Dot1l regulates GLTs expression fidelity” and Figure 5 “Global alteration in
transcription output caused by Dot1l loss” touch upon complex subjects that are not well integrated into
the main storyline. Figure 3 results are related to the regulation of gene expression plasticity by several

We appreciate the suggestions. We have restructured the manuscript based on the new data and
reviewers comments to improve the integration of all data.

covered in the Xiao et al review. However, we also show that the effects on the GLTUs are independent

The Figure 5 subject is complex and not limited to the role of DOT1L in Pol II pause release. There is
literature connecting DOT1L to enhancer regulation through effects on chromatin compaction, as well as

This point is no longer applicable to the revised manuscript, where we report direct effects on
transcription elongation rate that overlap with H3K79me3 content. We do not analyze enhancers or

I do not find conclusions that gene length affects the mode of transcription regulation by DOT1L (UP or
DOWN) particularly convincing, this part should be removed from the model in Figure 8 (or from the
manuscript altogether). Data analyses based on gene function might be more informative, especially if
related to the main story of the manuscript.
We have removed this consideration from the model. The observation that downregulated genes tend to
be longer than upregulated genes has been reported (Cao et al, 2020) and we find the same in DOT1L-
deficient CH12 and primary B cells (Fig. S4C). We only briefly mention this but make clear we do claim the
gene length affects how DOT1L regulates transcription but rather that long genes may be more sensitive

The authors relate their Pol II pause-release findings to literature about known pausing factors and their
inhibitors: Spt5, RN7SK, NELF, PAF1, etc. This is not justified by the results. Unless they do experiments and
implicate these factors in CSR, they must instead focus on the similarity of their DOT1L findings to the C.
elegans system that lacks NELF and the Wille et al. 2022, BioRxiv publication.
This was indeed not clearly written. SPT5, PAF1, SPT6, have been previously implicated in CSR. This was
referenced but not directly stated. Nonetheless, as the new data now indicates that the effect on pausing
is secondary to the direct increase in transcription elongation speed upon DOT1L loss, this was removed
from the Discussion.

5. The introduction gives no background about DOT1L and the current state of our understanding of its

We agree with the reviewer. We wrote the original manuscript from our chronological perspective of
finding DOT1L by AID BioID. At this stage this is no longer relevant, and we provide background on DOT1L

Specific issues:
Figure 4A, C: How does total RNA Pol II distribution look in Dot1l +/- conditions?
If the reviewer refers to Dot1l+/- heterozygous CH12F3 cells we did not analyze them. We obtained a single

If this refers to RNAPII distribution in WT vs KO cells we have now performed ChIP-seq (instead of

metagenes and screenshots are in Figs. 5 to 7 for different gene subsets.
Figure 4B, bottom: Why ChIP-qPCR at the P region is not shown?
We have remade these analyses (Fig. 7F, S7F). We bring to the attention of the reviewer that S-regions
show atypical pausing, with a broad RNAPII enrichment through the gene, instead of a narrow promoter-

affects AID occupancy, we focused on the segment of higher AID occupancy in the S-regions.
Figure 4C: Analyses using randomized groups of genes with the same # should be performed for control.
We think there was a misunderstanding. This figure showed all expressed genes stratified in quintiles by
their H3K79me3 (now Fig. S3F). The original figure also showed S2P-RNAPII heatmaps for the quintiles,

Figure 4F: Show expression changes corresponding to each group of genes.
We now show gene expression for each H3K79me3 gene quintile in Fig. 4A, S4A.
Figure 6 A, C: The difference between H3K79me3 distribution in splenic B cells and CH12F3 cells is

This was intriguing for us too, but we are confident that this is not a technical artifact. As we explain in

fold more selective for me3. We note that the ChIP-seq profiles in primary B cells were done with the

So, cytokine stimulation is unlikely to explain the difference in profiles between splenic B cells and CH12F3

Figure R1: Screenshots of H3K79 methylation at the IgH of mouse naïve B cells. Track 1 and 2: H3K79me2 and me3 in naïve

ChIP-seq in CH12F3 cells was done without CIT so it is not influenced by cytokines. We further show by
ChIP-PCR that there is no change in H3K79me3 after CIT at the Igh (Fig. S2C). Importantly, CIT does not

While in CH12F3 the pattern of H3K79me2 and H3K79me3 are similar, they are not fully overlapping as

Given that DOT1L is distributive, the higher abundance of H3K79me3 in CH12 likely reflects higher DOT1L
activity in CH12F3 than primary B cells. We posit that this could be explained by the distinct differentiation

The CH12F3 cell line has little differentiation potential and can accumulate H3K79 methylation.
Figure S2 B: Why does CIT lead to H3K79me reduction?
This is not the case. Biological replicates show that there is no change in H3K79me3 upon CIT at the Igh
(now Fig. S2C).
Triplicate replicates should be shown for all RT-qPCR and ChIP-qPCR data.
We present triplicates for most RT-qPCR and ChIP-qPCR data. In two cases, the differences, or lack of

In this paper, the authors investigate the mechanism of DOT1L promoting AID-induced class switch
recombination (CSR) as well as “off-target” mutations. They applied BioID to identify nuclear AID-proximal
proteins that potentially contribute to AID-induced mutations. From the results, they identified DOT1L and
its associated proteins, as well as SEC as being specifically enriched in the AID interacting complex. To
evaluate the function of DOT1L they perform knockdown and knockout experiments and find that CSR is
inconsistently affected at germ line transcripts depending on locus and method of knockout. Since the local
effects at IgH do not show a trend based on characteristics of accumulated chromatin marks, they then
perform RNAPII ChIP-seq from which they conclude a correlation between promoter pause release and
H3K79me3 enrichment. Finally they perform experiments on cohesion accumulation that suggest a link It
has been reported that DOT1L is essential for B cell differentiation, but the authors provide insights into
the potential mechanisms that may be relevant.
We thank the Reviewer for recognizing our original contributions. The revised version has adjusted and
further improved the mechanistic insight.
Major points:
1. The first major claim of the manuscript is that DOT1L has a role in CSR ( Fig 1-3 )- which has been reported
before (EMBO Rep. from the Leeuwen lab). In that prior paper it was shown that DOT1L promotes somatic
hypermutation and lowered RNA Pol II occupancy at immunoglobulin variable region.
It was not our intention to claim that we were the first to report the involvement of DOT1L in CSR.
However, we recognize that the way we originally framed the manuscript, based on the chronology of our
own findings, gave that impression.
We have revised the Introduction to clearly cite the prior work from the Van Leeuwen laboratory on CSR
and from the Scharff laboratory on SHM. We now explicitly state their contributions to establishing the
role of DOT1L in antibody diversification. We also better highlight the novelty of our study:
i) Reporting the general role of DOT1L in facilitating AID activity not only at the Igh locus but also at
off-target genes.
ii) Providing mechanistic insights into DOT1L’s function through structure–function analyses and
epistasis experiments.
iii) Defining how loss of DOT1L affects transcription elongation dynamics and how this compromises
AID occupancy and, consequently, its activity, in Dot1l-deficient B cells. In addition, changes in
transcription kinetics can explain gene expression changes in Dot1l-deficient cell, which has not
been elucidate yet.
1.1 The results in this manuscript are inconsistent with the prior published results (Fig 1E showed a different
result at the same locations (Su)) and at different regions where shDOT1L can both increase or decrease
RNAPII occupancy (Fig 1E).
We thank the reviewer for this observation. We have removed Fig. 1E. That ChIP-qPCR experiment was
intended as "quick and dirty" comparison of the effects of different DOT1L and SEC subunits on RNAPII
occupancy. However, as it lacked replicates, we agree that it was not sufficiently robust for publication.
We have now conducted new experiments focusing on the effect of DOT1L loss on transcription: We
performed ChIP-seq for RNAPII and TT-seq to measure nascent transcription genome-wide relative to
occupancy at genes enriched for H3K79me3. Furthermore, our data also provides a cause for this apparent
decrease: it is a consequence of increased transcription elongation velocity following DOT1L loss (see
detailed response to Point 2).

clones, rather than a direct mechanistic effect of DOT1L loss on end-joining.

Activation Induced Deaminase (AID) is an essential factor that drives somatic hypermutation and class
switch recombination in B Cells leading to antibody diversification. It is well accepted that AID mutates
single strand DNA (ssDNA) sequences to generate point mutations during SHM (V gene sequence
mutations) and DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) to cause CSR. In the process of catalyzing CSR and SHM,
AID also incorporates SHM all across the B Cell genome (although at a much lower frequency), these
mutations are related with occurrence of germinal center derived B cell lymphomas. A puzzling and
important question is how does AID identify various DNA target sequences, at V genes and its target DNA
sequence across the B cell genome. Many past studies have related AID activity with transcription states
both at sense and antisense direction, secondary DNA structures like R-loops and G4s (that form during
transcription), epigenetics and genome architecture formation, etc. In this study, the Subramani et al.
proposes that the H3K79me1/2/3 inducing enzymes DOT1L induces AID recruitment to the B cell genome.
The authors also propose that DOT1L functions with a similar mechanism to cause CSR, DOT1L deficient
CH12F3 lines are also deficient in CSR. The authors show that DOT1L induces RNA polII promoter proximal
pausing to accumulate RNA polII at AID target DNA sequences to induce AID recruitment (AID binds to RNA
polII robustly and thus this is the likely mechanism). In this regard, the authors show that in absence of
DOT1L promoter proximal paused RNA polII levels decrease but S2 phosphorylated elongating RNA polII
increases in the gene body. Thus, this study also makes the argument that S2 phosphorylated RNA polII is
unlikely to recruit AID. Although some previous studies (cited in the manuscript) have investigated and
shown DOT1L’s role in AID recruitment and CSR, neither of these two studies suggested mechanisms similar
to that proposed in this manuscript. Please find below some suggestions that the authors could consider
as they revise the manuscript for publication. Overall, I feel this manuscript advances the field of AID
biology and also provide insights into transcription and promoter-proximal pausing mechanism.

This manuscript examines the role of the H3K79 methyltransferase Dot1L in transcription, class switch
recombination (CSR), and AID mistargeting in the genome. The authors identify Dot1L and other factors
including components of the super elongation complex as AID proximity factors in 293 cells. As the authors
summarize, it was previously known that Dot1L contributes to efficient CSR and somatic hypermutation
(SHM), but the mechanism of action was unknown. The authors also nicely summarize previous findings
linking Dot1L to defects in transcription and point out the limitations in those findings. This study
substantially extends previous work by showing that Dot1L regulates transcription by restraining Pol2
promoter proximal pause release (PPPR). The substantial data presented here and the similarities with
findings from other factors that negatively regulate PPPR provide a strong argument that the catalytic
activity of Dot1L (and likely H3K79me2/me3) help restrict PPPR. This and the other findings related to the
effects of Dot1L on transcription are the main strength of the manuscript.
The authors also make the claim (last sentence of abstract) that their findings have established that
regulated pause release is “a critical step for AID activity”. We do not agree. While the findings strengthen
the link between Dot1L (and its catalytic activity) and CSR and AID targeting, they do not establish
mechanism. Specifically, the findings establish a correlation between Dot1L-regulated Pol2 PPPR and
CSR/AID targeting, not a causal link. One alternative explanation among others is that methylated H3K79
is the key contribution of Dot1L, not the regulation of PPPR. We feel that the mechanistic advance offered
by this study regarding the role of Dot1L in CSR/AID targeting is significant but not definitive. This is the
primary limitation of the study. We emphasize that we find their model attractive and plausible; it simply
hasn’t been established. Is this required for publication in Nature Communications? That’s a judgement
call, though overall we would support publication without a requirement for substantial additional
experiments. At minimum, the manuscript needs to be rewritten to remove overly strong mechanistic
claims and to address alternative hypotheses.
If the authors decide to try to strengthen the link between dysregulated PPPR and AID targeting, they
might attempt to identify a factor(s) that reduces CSR/AID targeting and alters PPPR similarly to Dot1L but
does not reduce levels of methylated H3K79—this would substantially strengthen the correlation and
argue against a primary role for methylated H3K79. Their study identifies several candidates for study,
e.g., SEC components.
In other regards, the study is rigorous, thorough, and well written (which we appreciated; a pleasure to
read). The experiments are well designed and controlled, caveats are noted and addressed, and
conclusions are carefully stated for the most part. The Discussion is well crafted to put the findings in the
context of other work.
We were unable to identify many other weaknesses with this study.
We thank the Reviewer for the positive comments.
We agree that the original manuscript did not establish the mechanism by which DOT1L contributed to
AID activity. The revised manuscript incorporates substantial new data and corrections that support a
more detailed mechanistic model. The model directly links the H3K792m2/3 to regulating transcription
elongation velocity, which can explain how DOT1L facilitates the activity of AID.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1: The revised manuscript by Subramani et al, “DOT1L activity limits transcription elongation velocity and favors RNAPII pausing to enable mutagenesis by Activation Induced Deaminase”, is significantly improved and provides additional data and analyses convincingly supporting the main conclusions of the study. I am satisfied with the responses to my critiques. It is satisfying that the new finding of the effect of DOT1L-mediated methylation (likely of H3K79) on transcription elongation velocity can resolve some previously conflicting data. However, the newly found mechanism cannot explain all known cases of DOT1L regulating gene expression, especially those where the catalytic function does not play a role. I encourage the authors to leave room for such possibilities in the discussion. Some thoughts on how H3K79 methylation may slow down transcription elongation would also be interesting to include in the discussion.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript by Subramani et. al. the authors implicate DOT1L activity on AID activity for class switch recombination and somatic hypermutation. Several of the findings in the original manuscript have been removed, making this revision read like a new submission. The authors have significantly improved the readability of the manuscript and removed erroneous conclusions from the prior version that are mentioned in the rebuttal.

Major claims from the abstract
1.DOT1L deficiency causes mostly increased nascent transcription, accompanied by a modest reduction in RNAPII occupancy.
The relation between absolute (not relative to DOT1L KO) steady state gene expression, nascent expression and H3K79me3 quintiles can be made clearer by using heatmaps for each quintile. Currently it is unclear what happens to the ~50% of genes in Q1 that have increased nascent transcription but no change in steady state transcription. i.e. why does a change in nascent transcription not lead to change in steady state transcription- do they have very high absolute expression that cannot increase further?
2. DOT1L restricts the velocity of transcription elongation proportional to higher order H3K79 methylation (H3K79me2/3)
This effect of DOT1L on elongation velocity is known from other systems that they reference.
The data in Fig 6D that all genes irrespective of change in expression increase in elongation velocity upon DOT1L knockout is also consistent with the hypothesis that H3K79me3 is irrelevant to gene expression. Fig 6C (which is not referenced at all in the main text) would suggest that downregulated genes are limited by the amount of RNAPII that they can recruit, that is it is an RNAPII initiation problem. Therefore, the author’s claim of mechanistic insight into why some genes are downregulated upon DOT1L KO is somewhat premature.
3. The relationship between DOT1L and AID association and mutagenesis at target loci remain unclear
By the authors’ own statement “AID occupies far more genomic loci than it mutates, indicating that additional regulatory steps determine its activity in situ”. Similarly, DOT1L mediated H3K79 methylation occupies almost the entire transcribed genome. Yet only ~200 genes in B cells and 78 genes in the CH12F3 cell line are AID off targets. Even among these AID off targets, the genes behave like the rest of the H3K79me3 enriched genome in increasing elongation velocity upon DOT1L KO- leading to the question of whether DOT1L functions in a regulatory capacity.

Minor points
1. I am not in favor of the term “nuclear neighbors” – without a distance limit, any two nuclear proteins can be considered nuclear neighbors.
2. AID off-target genes exhibited significantly higher levels of H3K79me2 and H3K79me3 downstream of the transcription start site (TSS) compared to the control gene set (Fig. 3A, 3B).
These changes extremely small changes although statistically significant in B cells
3. 3E is not very useful because H3K79me is not normally distributed, unlike other histone modifications.
4. 3G lacks significance testing
5. In figure 4 What is 1ry?
6. Fig 4G CTCF is misspelled
4. In 7B are red and black lines switched for WT and DOT1L KO?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: All my relevant points have been addressed by the authors and the manuscript improved in clarity and in its coherence. I do not have other points to raise.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4: The authors have revised the manuscript adequately and have addressed concerns.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The authors have added substantial data and significantly revised the manuscript, leading to a revised model for the role of DOT1L in AID action focusing on restraining transcription elongation velocity. Reduced pausing downstream of the TSS in the absence of DOT1L is now interpreted as a secondary effect. The findings are rigorous and well-presented and carefully discussed. While much more molecular detail remains to be discovered regarding the mechanism by which the action of AID is coordinated with Pol2 transcription, the model proposed by the authors is provocative, plausible, consistent with the data, and will serve as a useful guidepost for future studies. A distinct and particular strength of the revised manuscript is the substantial insights it provides regarding the role of DOT1L and H3K79me2/3 in regulating Pol2 transcription, providing a new conceptual framework that helps make sense of a previously confusing literature. The level of advance and insight provided is easily sufficient for publication. Because the paper proposes a new model for DOT1L function, it would be easy to ask for more detailed mechanism but this would not be appropriate given the scope of findings and insights provided already in this paper.

Minor:
1. Typos on lines 266 and 440.
2. Line 464: I was puzzled by the phrase “despite only”, since increased elongation velocity and decreased Pol2 “push” in opposite directions. Wouldn’t “accompanied by” be better, since decreased Pol2 emphasizes and supports the finding of increased velocity?
